Forrestal, I go 4th, on my second turn I play him.

the caveat, "damn we're gonna contest" and "sorry man gotta do it"
and "deck is based on Ian".

know my game is FUBAR.

vampires, especially 8 cap vampires.

It is such an incredibly random event that it takes someone with many
years of playing to have even experienced it enough to form an opinion
on it.

Messages.Author: D.J.
Messages.Body:
On Aug 10, 5:00 pm, henrik <www.hen...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Yeah. If the contest did nothing else than making you both lose it's
> your predator's stupidness that got you there. I think the problem is
> mostly that your deck couldn't handle being without Ian.

I don't see Norm saying anywhere that *his* deck, being the one who
brought out Ian first, couldn't function without Ian.

What he said is that his predator, who decided *his* deck couldn't
function without Ian, contested after Norm brought him out but before
even doing anything with him. Yes, that's debatably an asshat move,
but if predator hadn't done that, he's 7 pool down the tubes for a few
turns and waiting a few more before he gets a real vampire up.
(Similar to how Ben Kalb's deck, in that other ludicrously long
thread, would have been just fine with a different vampire than Lutz,
but was already 10 pool into getting Lutz ready to be out, so when
Lutz then popped up cross table Ben was screwed whether or not he
contested and thus screwed the other guy too.)

Whether or not Norm needed Ian, specifically, once Ian was on the
table and then got contested, what Norm needed was the 8 pool
investment, plus the cost of contesting, plus the 2 turns, back. The
rules provide no way of doing that. Let's assume Norm's predator
picked the other option, and didn't contest - what he needed was some
way to get back the investment before he just plain lost, then. Which
doesn't exist, because contesting is too harsh.

> I'm not saying contesting didn't make your situation worse. It did,
> and I think contesting is supposed to work exactly that way. If you
> couldn't handle not having Ian for 4 turns, that's not at all a rules
> problem. Really.

OK, how's this: whatever your first, fairly large, vampire is, you're
1 pool shy of bringing it out. And it pops up cross-table. Not a
star for you, not a specific highly-popular vampire, just random
chance. You're 8 pool into a 9-cap or something. How is that not a
rules problem totally screwing your game over on pure randomness?

> People contesting for no reason are the same people that stealthes
> through a bounced bleed and ousts crosstable because the "need to
> cycle cards". Or that burns their grand predator's Ian with Goratrix
> Adv.

And people that choose not to contest the vampire they've started
putting pool onto just lose on their own, without taking someone with
them, but that's still a big pile of no-fun, and unnecessarily harsh.

- D.J.

understand how debilitating it is. How would you feel if the rule was
changed to "All capacities are unique, if two vampires of the same
capacity are brought into play then they contest"? I think that you
would come to grips with it quite quickly if you experienced it more.
Then you could strategically use contesting by playing skill cards on
your vampires.

There is the transfer back rule, you know. I heard it was created for

> > I'm not saying contesting didn't make your situation worse. It did,

A week back, in a casual game, my grand predator put up Anson. My
predator played an Ansons deck as well. He changed vampire, got Volker
and Nik out, rushed Anson and sent him to torpor and then ate Anson.
Then he brought his own copy out and won the game.

> How is that not a
> rules problem totally screwing your game over on pure randomness?

The game is about getting over randomness. When you build your deck
you should consider the things you might encounter and design your
deck to be able to handle as many as possible of those. Sometimes you
will end up facing a deck that you can't handle. That's part of the
game, and you have to try solving it from the crapplace you're in. You
can build your deck so that it can handle a contest, and if you chose
not to then you will most likely lose when the situation comes up.
Just like you can build your deck so that it can handle an Animalism
weenie, and if you chose not to then you will most likely lose when
that one is your prey.
Change your deck and playing style instead of the rules.

> > People contesting for no reason are the same people that stealthes
> > through a bounced bleed and ousts crosstable because the "need to
> > cycle cards". Or that burns their grand predator's Ian with Goratrix
> > Adv.
>
> And people that choose not to contest the vampire they've started
> putting pool onto just lose on their own, without taking someone with
> them, but that's still a big pile of no-fun, and unnecessarily harsh.

And people who get their first vampire Brainwashed after 7 transfers
can lose as well. Let's ban Brainwash. Cairo Airport Caitiff decks
should be illegal as well.
Or they could just get a different vampire out and do the best of the
situation. And also consider that some tables are almost impossible to
win (due to the random seating ending up giving you the "wrong"
predator/prey/grand prey/grand predator.
If you have the wrong deck in the wrong situation it'll suck. What
situation is wrong depends on how what your deck was constructed to
handle.
But yeah, one could just blame the rules instead.

> If you have the wrong deck in the wrong situation it'll suck. What

> handle.
> But yeah, one could just blame the rules instead.

The contesting rule for crypt minions is indeed very harsh. The
penalty for falling victim to this very random event is the (at least
temporary) loss of a minion, the time invested in controlling that
minion (that could have been used to control a different one), the
investment of Pool for that minion, and continued loss of that minion
and additional Pool for the duration of the contest. There is a high
probability that the table will tilt drastically in favor of
methuselahs NOT involved in the contest, for no other reason than that
the contest exists.

Saying that one should "build their library or crypt to deal with" a
contest is not fair, IMO, because that means using your very limited
resources to defend against something that is very unlikely. Do you
play clan hosers in all your decks? You should, because you will
probably see vampires that belong to clans in every game. Not having a
clan hoser card for every clan in every deck is folly!

My apologies for the sarcasm, but I think the fact that the punishment
for contesting may not fit the crime has to be considered.

What if the contestation rules for unique crypt minions (NOT unique
library cards) were more along the lines of a Hostile Takeover? When a
minion is contested, the involved methuselahs bid for control of that
minion (starting with the methuselah who already controlled the
minion). The winning bid is paid in Pool to the yielder, who then
removes their in-play copy of the minion from the game, and burns any
cards or counters that may have been on that minion.

This accomplishes a few things:

-It resolves the contest immediately

-It provides some measure of compensation for the yielder

-It adds an additional element of strategy to contesting a crypt
minion

-It does not "undo" time and resources invested without compensation

It also uses a mechanic that is familiar to most players, and has been
around a long time.

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
Wasn't there just another very long post on this very subject? I
guess it's touched a nerve.

Maybe instead of contesting, whenever you bring out a unique minion
from your uncontrolled region, if there is already a copy of that
minion, the other controller's copy gets sent back to the uncontrolled
region like a Banishment. I'm sure this was suggested before, as were
a multitude of ideas for dealing with the situation. Something like
this really plays along to the theme of VTES - a tug of war between
Methusalehs over the control of a vampire.

In my play group in LA, I have seen the contestation issue come up
four times in memory:
1. A complete newbie contested my Masika. I was playing a Masika star
vampire deck. He didn't realize what would happen once his Masika
came out. Nonetheless, he was in the same position as has been
discussed - if he hadn't contested Masika, he still would have lost
several turns and transfers.
Of course, after he gave up the contestation, I got an Assault Rifle
on Masika and my prey then used Serpentis to bring the other Masika
out of the ash heap to contest him. I had to play kill through
contestation as best I could. The game timed out, I think. I never
in my life imagined that I would have to contest Masika.

2. A predator contested his prey's Gabrin. Both were ousted without
gaining VPs.

3. My predator didn't bring out Anson because I already had him. It
hurt his game a lot, but he could still function. I won the game. He
couldn't or wouldn't contest because his predator was a stealth
bleeder.

4. Someone else contested my Anson cross table just cause I think he
was frustrated with the game and he didn't understand the contestation
rules. Once he realized he couldn't get blood back from a contested
vampire and I was going to pay the contest to the bitter end, he gave
up. I got 1 VP that game.

Hmm... Maybe this contestation thing isn't that rare after all. I
would guess it happens in 5% of games. Doing something a little more
dynamic than the current rules might be worth considering.

I think the main problem of this discussion is that many players don't
understand deckbuilding. You build your deck, play it, and then get
screwed. You then have 2 options when analysing why you lost.

it's not a matter of you having to improve yourself.

good players use them to their advantage.

good for me to contest and when it's bad for me to contest. Current
rules are in my opinion very good since they add strategic depth and
presents you with problems that are very hard to solve, but still
quite solvable.

Messages.Author: Drace
Messages.Body:
Considering table dynamics, I think unless you're up against a
stubborn predator or poor cross table player, contesting is fine.

As the prey, you should be able to table talk your predator, "We can
contest X or I can choose not to influence him out if you give me X
turns of relief."
As predator, you can use the same table talk for your prey, "I won't
go forward for X turns, if you choose not to contest."

As someone on this newsgroup here said, contesting IS a choice. You
cannot influence out both minions in the same turn if it's two
different players. Even IF you're hosed cross table, you're not
hopeless as you have cross table allies. No one wants to see their
grandprey getting walked over if they can help it.

Regarding illogical plays/asshat behaviors, well that comes down to
VTES's problem. Yes you can lose games due to unforeseen plays that
you don't agree with. But guess what? At a tournament, you just have
to deal. Unless you ban all players that hasn't attained X level of
skill, it will happen.

And yet the contestation rules are a big part of it. You change the
contestation rules so that contestation has a less severe penalty (but

useful. Which seems to be a current blanket design goal.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Peter D Bakija" <pd...@lightlink.com> wrote in message
news:1c6fd272-c875-4ebd...@p15g2000vbl.googlegroups.com...


It looks to me like people are talking past each other about the intent
or utility of contestation (apart from simply encouraging diversity by
forbidding the simultaneous use of, say, multiple Arika decks on the same
table). Sure, contestation can be seen purely as a drawback in the
metagame against star vampire decks. And it's absolutely true that other
useful rules also have unintended and undesirable side effects at times,
just like contestation. But there's clearly no metagame need to hose
star vampire decks given that their vulnerability to so many other game
effects (destroyed by combat, Pentex Subversion and other effects of that
sort, "minion-cannot-block/block-fails" forms of stealth, and probably a
number of other things I'm not thinking of right at this moment) really
does a fine job of keeping them from being overrepresented in the
metagame. Does anyone disagree with this? I mentioned in the other
discussion about Heir to the Blood reprints that I agreed Carlton Van
Wyck should get reprinted in part because the occasional contestation
of Carlton is a useful check on his general utility. But are there
people who actually believe that certain star vampires need the same
check? That would strike me as extreme.

If not, then the question simply boils down to: "Are the occasional
hosed-up games that contestation can lead to when two star vampire decks
collide common enough and bad enough to call for a change to the
contestation rules?" The main drawbacks to changing the rules are
the confusion caused by changing existing rules and possibly creating
significantly more complex rules in a game already seen as too complex
by many.

In my book, the bad games caused by contestation are too rare to reach
the threshold of tempting me to tinker with the rules. But I don't
blame people for disagreeing because I know the games where this has
an effect can be pretty rude.

Fred

>
> I don't think he is either. I think it's because changing the rules is
> the easy way out, instead of adjusting deck building and play style to
> be able to handle contesting better.

"Easy" is kind of a perjorative word here. I would say your answer to it
misses his point and that's why the two of you are talking past each other.
When solving general game problems, the answer is always to change the rules
of the game, as opposed to expecting invididuals changing their style of
play. The problem of unfun games caused by contesting star vampires is a
systemic problem; in competitions, the role of individuals is merely to do
the best they can at winning games. They are not responsible for making the
game more fun if, for instance, their best strategy turns out to be one
that creates less fun games.

To give you a much more apparent example of what I mean, if VtES is _much_
easier to win by players using stealth-bleed decks than combat decks, the
answer to print new cards and/or ban old cards in order to allow for a
more balanced metagame, which is presumedly more fun. (Note that banning,
changing, and printing cards are merely another means of changing the
rules to a game - since card text are essentially game rules in a CCG.)
Notice that the answer to making the game more balanced is contained in
a change to the game, not an expectation that players should engage in
sub-optimal strategies. If you're responding to what is seen as a problem
in contestation creating unfun games by telling people to alter the
strategies they would otherwise pursue, you're essentially doing the same
thing: expecting player to engage in sub-optimal strategies to solve a
game problem. Wrong. Fix the game itself and let players be free to
choose the strategies they think best for their chances of winning without
worrying about whether those strategies cause crippled games.

(To avoid misunderstanding, again: my personal view is that contestation-
crippled games aren't frequent enough to bother. But that's a different
objection.)

> I think contesting should be the biggest fear for star vampire decks.

It is not and never has been. Destruction or otherwise rendering useless
the star vampire is almost certainly the biggest downside to star vampire
decks. Second, I suppose, would be the usual metagame risks that all decks
are subject to, whether star vampires are used or not. Also in there
somewhere is the chance of not drawing your star vampire, if the crypt is
mixed. Contestation, in my observation, is really quite a rare problem.
(And hence this is why I hold my opinion about the merits of changing these
rules.) It just has massive effects on the game when it happens. And
the negative effects Peter is complaining about go beyond simply one or two
guys losing a game.

> They should be built to be able to handle it or, if they're not built
> to handle it, they shouldn't expect to win as much. It's very possible
> to build star vampire decks that still can manage to play games without
> their star.

That's your personal view of strategy. Another reasonable view is that
the possibility isn't worth covering and trying to cover it will weaken
your star vampire deck too much. So accept defeat when it happens and
win more often in the vast majority of cases when it doesn't happen.

But such a view doesn't solve Peter's perceived problem of contestation
causing unfun games. Again, the job of players is do their best to win.
It's the job of the rules to create the greatest possibility that the games
will be fun.

Fred

If that is indeed the only real reason behind these endless discussions
about changing contest rules, why don't we just play with open uncontrolled
regions? Is there any *real* argument not to do so? I'm not too pursuaded by
the strategical "keep my vampire hidden" argument as that's generally out of
the window in turn 2. Besides, in any tournament with, say, less than 20
people (which is the large majority) this secrecy is a virtually
non-existant in rounds beyond the first. Plus, it could be argued that being

strategic counter-play instead of just getting out the guy you planned to,

something legal. Note that I'm not saying this is a problem anywhere I have
played. On the contrary even, but it's surely a lot "cleaner" and less prone
to mistakes. Mistakes that usually require significant judge interference to
correct.

Of course, we're not going to play with open uncontrolled regions anytime
soon, leading me to believe there is more behind all this than *just* the
oddball "I got contest-fucked out of the game randomly".

On Aug 12, 10:00 am, "Izaak" <nom...@usenet.plz> wrote:
...

> The underlying question that I'm reading in it, is why the dozen of other
> ways of getting your game fubar'd are acceptable and not in need of a change
> and contestation (apparently) is.

I do see the following things all sit in the category of "stuff that
will bone my game horribly but I can't really do much about when they
actually happen that I haven't already done before I sat down to play
VTES"

- Seating order
- Library Jam
- Crypt Screw/Jam

Seating Order
Seating order, more often than not, leads to a more-frequent less-fun
VTES experience. Getting the deck archetype that you have least
defence for as a predator sucks, but that was something I defended
least against when I built the deck... long before I sat down to
play. My issue, it was a risk I assessed as low and didn't protect
heavily against it.

Library Jam/Crypt Screw
I shuffled, the cards got cut and unadulterated chance screwed me. My
combat deck drew all of its masters/action mods and none of the rushes
and combat cards...
My vote deck drew no vote-push...
My superstar deck drew all of the Support Cast
and so on...
Again... pure bald-faced chance of the same variety as seating. Did
all of my planning to avoid this by the way I designed the library/
crypt.

Contesting
Wow, I landed on a table with another Eurotrash-Brujah deck and looks
like we both want Donal OConnor... bugger, bollocks and damnation.
Looks like I work on getting Constanza out first and we can have a
debate about Theo during someone else's turn while we don't have to
care so much about what is happening...
UNLIKE the others this involves Chance + Choice. Chance = landing on
another table where someone will want to utilise the same vampire.
Choice = both of you choosing to influence that vampire out. DURING
THE GAME I had the opportunity to avoid this situation, it didn't just
rely on choices I made BEFORE I sat down and certainly required
choices made by others AFTER I sat down.

So, by combining the fact that it requires a number of player's
choices, occurs during the game and occurs comparatively rarely, I
squarely fall in the camp for:
"The Contesting Rule Does Not Need To Be Changed"

> prey's
> last vampire and uses the lack of interceptors to bleed the guy out.)

A situation that, on paper, should be (almost) as rare as the random event
of your 1-blood-short minion getting brought out crosstable out of your
control. How often do you *really* get the chance to contest someone's last
blocker without him seeing it coming or at least him being able to get some
clue. I mean, it's not as if you randomly throw a Carna in a Setite deck
just in case your prey might play a Carna Superbowl wall. I mean, sure, I
see that happening for Carltons, Ivory Bows, Hearts of Cheat and
Aranthebeses all the time, but crypt cards? Serious?

> difference
> enough of the time that I like it as a feature in the game, myself.

Oh I don't neccesarily disagree. I don't think contestation rules need to be
changed because the random event that's being discussed is simply too rare
to go and fiddle with the rules. But if you're looking to fix said
occurance, it should be made sure to fix only THAT specific occurance
instead of messing about with new transfer and influence rules as suggested
in the 700-post thread a week or what ago.

> 2) Face up uncontrolled minions would hardly be a costless solution as you
> suggest. At least, not IMHO.

Maybe not. I think it might actually actually encourage people to build more
varied crypts with different capacity ranges so that one is able to respond
to his or her predators and prey's crypts instead of going into "no brain
influence out Lutz"-mode for the first 3 turns and hoping nobody else had
the same idea.

Or you could say that the 4 initial cryptcards are face up at the start of
the game and at the start of player 1's master phase phase all cards in the
uncontrolled regions are shuffled and put back face down. Proceed as current
afterwards. Plenty options. What I'd like to see, if a rule change is deemed
to be required, is a clean and easy to understand one. Preferably in one
sentence and it should fix exactly the situation we've been discussing all
along without causing all kinds of collateral damage (such as the new
transfer rules that were brought in that other thread would IMO cause).

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Assume distinct vampires in each individual uncontrolled region (otherwise the
math gets complicated).

Player A:
V1, V2, V3, V4 (100% chance of getting 4 vampires).

Player B:
1263/1267 * 1262/1266 * 1261/1265 * 1260/1264 = 98.74% miss (not getting any of
the four vampires A has).

Including all other players B,C,D,E (all missing the players that went before):

Definition of the falling factorial (the first n terms of a factorial):
ff(x,n) := x!/(x-n)! = x * (x-1) * (x-2) * ... * (x-n+1)

ff(1263,16) / ff(1267,4)^4 = 88.07% miss

Over all 8 tables:
(ff(1263,16) / ff(1267,4)^4)^8 = 36.19% miss

Meaning 63.81% chance of at least one table with at least two players sharing at
least one vampire between them.

... in the first round.

Over three rounds (assuming the 4 vampires drawn in the earlier rounds have no
bearing on the ones drawn in later rounds):
(ff(1263,16) / ff(1267,4)^4)^8^3 = 4.74% miss

Meaning 95.26% chance of at least one uncontrolled-region collision in three rounds.

(not including the final)

> Oooooh, strong logic rebuttal......

>1267 unique vampires. Lets assume the people playing all chose their
> vampires out of this group. Leaving aside non unique minions for the

> a tournament with 40 players.

> someone please do the actual stats as to 2 people sitting down at a
> table with the exact same vamp in their opening crypt draw.

I can't do the numbers of what you asked on the fly, but let's give this a
go:

With 1267 vampires in the pool, we assume that all vampires are equally
likely to see play which is simply not true. For simplicity�s sake let�s
assume only 900 vampires actually see play - this is a purely arbitrary
number that I felt is reasonable. Now, the odds of someone influencing to
the same vampire as you in turn 1 is 1 in 900, or 0,11 %. Or rather, the
odds of him NOT transferring to the same guy are 99,89%. Of course there are
3 more players, so that makes the chance that nobody else is influencing to
the same vampire as you are 0,9989^4 = 0,9956 or approximately 99,6%.

If we account for the fact that other players might influence to the same
vampire that is different from yours and that it happening to them would
make the game equally unfun for you, the odds of everything going to plan do
drop a bit, and round to 99,5%. This isn't too surprising as the difference
between 1 in 900, 1 in 899 and 1 in 898 is neglicable.

So what we have is a 99,5% chance of not seeing this "random crosstable fuck
of someone bringing out the guy someone else was transferring to", which
means that it happens on average once in 200 tables. Of course a tournament
with 40 players (3R+F) has a total of 25 tables played so the chance of this
random crosstable "contest before you bring it out" is 1-(0,995^25) = 0,117.
Which is roughly 12% chance. Of course, looking at the TWDA, most
tournaments don't have anywhere near 40 players, but more like 15-25
players. Let's assume 25 (which is a high estimate) player tournaments,
which have only 16 tables played. In that scenario the odds of it happening
on any table during the day are only 7,7%.

So, on average, if you play 5 tournaments a year, this would happen once
every 3 years *in a tournament you're playing* not even neccesarily on a
table you're playing. That chance is a mere 2,0% per tournament played,
assuming you make the finals in all of them. Again, going with 5 tournaments
a year it would occur once every 25 years on average.

And that's with a pool of 900 crypt cards. In reality, of course, this is
only a real problem with the bigger minions (say, 6+?) reducing the odds
even more in favor of it not happening. Do we *really* need a rulechange for
that?

I can see that contesting key vampires in your decks is a topic that
some players have strong feelings about. I have been the victim of
this before in a qualifier and I didn’t have a problem with it.

As the game currently stands I believe there is a good balance of
player skill, both in deck building and actual play during the game,
along with luck of the draw which helps to keep the game fresh and
exciting each time you play with a deck. Without this VTES would be no
different from any other card games out there.

9/10 times they already know there going to win or louse because there
playing a particular deck. Also I believe the concern of contesting to
some extent helps to keep a verity of decks to see play. If everyone
played the same deck this game would get old really quick.

add cards to your deck that will help you get out your vampires faster
and have other good uses later in the game such as Dreams of the
Sphinx. If someone else decides to contest with you it’s likely a
strategic decision and there is not much you can do about that.

For me its part of the game I love to play, and sometimes that means
taking the good with the bad.

>I welcome any evidence to the contrary of my position (evidence that

While it is difficult for me to prove what the original designers
intended beyond the shadow of a doubt (especially since i didn`t start
playing until much later or interact with any of them in any way),
Consider the following:

The transfer back rule appears in the original Jyhad rulebook.
This means that the rule has been with us since the the first set,
which also gave us quite a large Number of Cards that put blood on
uncontrolled vampires (six total, by my count).
I posit that designers/playtesters could hardly have missed the
interaction between theses Cards and the transfer back rule.
Thus it is likely that they approved of this interaction (or at least
did not strongly disapprove of it), since it would have been trivial
to restrict reverse transfers to copies of vampires already in play to
limit/stop such bloat.
(There was even another opportunity with the Vtes set, but to my
Knowledge it was not taken, despite there being several alterations in
the transition)

Interstingly, the example in the rulebook explaining the transfer back
rule doesn`t mention contesting but instead the player (Nora) deciding
that putting pool on that Vampire was a mistake.
(Just as an aside, such mistakes seem a pretty good reason to have a
transfer back rule. It is after all no more fun to lose pool to a
mistransfer than it is to lose it to a possible contest)

There is also the original Wording of Brainwash, which only stops
transfers to that minion, not off him.

All these things lead me to believe that the Designers considered the
Rule a seperate part of the ruleset even though it may have been
originally created to avoid contests. (or to allow a player to correct
his mistakes in influecing for that matter).

I was also going to reference that example. Since you already have,
I'll run with it:

Even if contestation never occured, players would occasionally find
themselves in situations like Nora's, where they have begun to
influence a vampire, but due to changing circumstances between turns,
decide against it. The transfer back rule allows a player to adapt to
these changes during the game at something of a cost - recouping the
pool investment takes twice as long as making investment did, and
doing so limits the player's ability to influence a different minion.
This is true whether the change of circumstances is due to the
potential for contestation, new information about your opponents'
capabilities, or significant loss of pool during your predator's turn
- and even if contestation is removed as a factor, the others remain.

Also, we've also had 15 years of card with the rules as they are.
Presumably that side effect of bloat through the uncontrolled region
was taken into consideration during design and playtest. For example,
Public Trust would be significantly less useful in the absence of a
transfer-back rule, while Legal Manipulations would suffer not at all.

-witness1

online rulebook says:

"Nora comes to her influence phase. She has four transfers to spend,
but only 2 pool. She sees that she has built up 8 blood counters on a
vampire with a blood capacity of 10, and she thinks she can win the
game if she gets it into play. However, she cannot use both counters
in her pool to put it into play because that would put her out of the
game. She had invested a couple of blood counters in a vampire with a
blood capacity of 7 on a previous turn, so she spends two of her four
transfers to take back 1 of those counters and put it in her pool. Now
she has 3 pool and two transfers left to spend. She spends the two
transfers by moving 2 of the 3 blood counters from her pool to the
vampire with the blood capacity of 10 and moves that vampire to the
ready region."

OK. These threads are too massive to go back and study every punch and
counterpunch. I'm just saying, the distinction is important and I see pretty
strong evidence that you're missing it. Or that you're missing some
important implications that come from it.

> > But here's the problem: you're responding to the wrong original complaint,

This is exactly the reasoning that I believe is causing you to conflate
the two. You may be correct about this but the fact is, players build
decks to win games and they SHOULD build decks to win games. They are
not tasked with the responsibility of building decks to make the games
fun. The rules of the game are supposed insure that. Well, OK, no game
rules can insure such a thing but it's better if they're comported to
insure the best chance of having a fun game.

Your words above indicate that you're placing the burden of fun-ness on
the individual players, and stating that a player should compose his deck
towards the goal increasing the fun-ness of the game - at the expense of
what he might feel is his best chance to actually win the game. The
trouble with this is that fun-ness is a group goal, not an individual
goal. And even if I compose my deck torwards maximum fun-ness, another
player (say my grand-prey) might not, preferring to go for optimizing for
victory. And when his stab at victory goes awry because he's contesting
Enkidu with his prey, then my prey waltzes in and grabs two easy victory
point. No fun for me and here I did nothing bad. I weakened my deck
by making sure I had alternatives to Stanislava in case anyone else
brought her out but no one did, so now I've got a weaker deck and an
unfun game. Oh, well...

> Just like a game can become unfun for an imbued deck when it gets
> Stanislava for predator. If you run into something that's totally
> impossible to handle (I know imbueds can handle Stanislava in some
> ways, just an example) then the game tend to become less fun.

Sure. But that's a different issue and not one that anyone's trying
to solve. It's not a valid argument to say, "The game is flawed in
this way and we can't fix that so we shouldn't try to fix anything."
Had LSJ taken such an attitude when Return To Innocence was a problem,
it would still be part of the game.

> However, it doesn't get heavily unfun until the player throws in the
> towel and gives up.

Well, actually that's not true. Games can easily become unfun whether
a player in a terrible position gives up or not. But such a nit is
beside the point and not worth bickering over.

Fred

The way I look at it, when building decks, is that I try to cover as
many possible match ups as I can think of. I try to make my decks good
vs bleed decks, vote decks, combat decks, wall decks, weenie decks,
high cap decks and so on. When doing that I also tend to think about
contesting, since there's a risk that I'll end up at a table where
someone else plays the same minion/s as I am.
I don't know why you think I do this because I want the other players
at my table to have fun. I do it because the deck gets better. I do it
to win.

But of course, most decks won't be good against every other deck.
They'll have a weakness of some kind. What that weakness is, is
something you chose when building the deck. You can chose to make it
great against bleed decks and vote decks while skipping combat
defense. Just like you can make your deck great against combat decks
and bleed decks while skipping vote defense.
Those are choices you make. And whether you do them to win or to bring
fun-ness to the table isn't something I really my concern. You're free
to do it because the monster in your basement told you to (not saying
you're crazy and talks with basement monsters, just an example).

Now, if I think I'll have a big risk of contesting one or more of the
vampires in my crypt, the first thing I'd do is to switch deck. The
second thing I'd do (if I really, really wanted to play with that clan/
minion) is to make sure that I can survive an early contest. Crypt
acceleration, low/mid cap vampires, bloat cards and stuff like that
can help here. I don't see this as a sub-optimal thing to do with my
deck. If I saw it that way, I wouldn't do it.

And, as I've stated before, constructing your deck so that it can
handle your first minion being removed from the game rather fast is a
great thing when it comes to deck building. It doesn't make the deck
weaker. It doesn't necessarily make the other players have more fun
(it's quite likely to make you have more fun though, since a good deck
is more fun to play).
It's good, since on many tables something bad will happen early on. It
could be a War Ghoul, Pentex Subversion, Mind Rape + diableri, contest
or whatever. The list is huge, and being prepared for crap stuff like
that will give you a good edge when they happen.

> > Just like a game can become unfun for an imbued deck when it gets
> > Stanislava for predator. If you run into something that's totally
> > impossible to handle (I know imbueds can handle Stanislava in some
> > ways, just an example) then the game tend to become less fun.

> Sure.  But that's a different issue and not one that anyone's trying
> to solve.  It's not a valid argument to say, "The game is flawed in
> this way and we can't fix that so we shouldn't try to fix anything."
> Had LSJ taken such an attitude when Return To Innocence was a problem,
> it would still be part of the game.

That's not my point. I don't think the Stanislava vs Imbueds is a real
flaw. It's just an example of how a game sometimes can be very bad,
due to the randomness of seating. I think that's fine, in a game like
this. Random seating will make my deck easier or harder to play. There
are many, many tables I walk away from with 0 vps and say "there
wasn't much I could do about that with my deck, considering what I was
up against". But just because I couldn't do anything about those other
decks doesn't mean the rules should be changed to make it easier on
the deck I played.

I do think that if the contest rule is so horrible, then Stanislava vs
Imbueds is a huge problem. As well as Pentex Subversion, Sense Dep.,
Brainwash, War Ghouls, Renegade Garous etc.
All those things can ruin your game after just 3-4 turns, unless
you're prepared to handle them. Just like a contest can.
If Return To Innocence had been a dominate card that had a cost of 1
and said "(d) bleed at +2 bleed", I would've agreed with your
comparision.

in the long run to try to cover every possiblity (as you yourself noted
further down in your post). In some cases, at least, it would certainly
weaken a deck overall to attempt to cover the possibility that your star
vampire is contested. Ergo, a player may quite reasonably conclude that
his best choice is to build as if he will never be contested - and just
write off the games when he is as lost causes. And so expose any game in

players to construct and/or play their decks correctly. But while the
two goals certainly have a relationship, ultimately they're different
things. So I believe that remains the source of your disagreement with

> "transfer-back" has gained a place of its own distinct from "losing-
> the-contestation-lottery" and therefore should be handled (if at all)
> on its own and not in some sort of bundle.

While I completely agree with you, that "contestation" can be fixed
without touching "undo influence" (I'm still standing on the side of
"if you yield contestation, you get all the blood on the contested
minion put back into your pool" as the simplest, cleanest, most laser
guided repair with the least collateral damage), I can see where LSJ
is (at least I think I do) coming from here--if you fix contestation,
the game rules are not at a zero sum relative to now. Something is
just changed, and the thing that was introduced into the game to
balance that out, still being there, leaves the game in an unbalanced
state. So removing the "undo influence" is the cost for fixing
"contestation". I don't know if this would be a positive change to the
game (as contestation, while sucky, *is* random and fairly infrequent
while transferring back is incredibly common and would affect most
games all the time). But I can see why the connection is made and the
two are lumped together.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Mathieu Rivero
Messages.Body:
I had contesting issues on my last game, on Dmitra Ilyanova. My prey
played it before I could say a word and this was totally unexpected.
Now how could I get the vote lock? By contesting. But this messed up
the game for both he and I. But I didn't whine.

Now, it's true that contesting most of the time ruins two players,
especially on high capacity vampires. I'd like to make a suggestion to
LSJ : let's not change contesting rules, but add a new influence rule.

During your influence phase, spend 4 transfers to move all blood on a
contested minion to one of your uncontrolled vampire or imbued. Remove
the contested minion from the game.

This allows several game mechanics about contesting :
> contesting is still bad. If no one yields, pool keeps to be lost. (outcome : keeps game diversity)
> contesting slows contested vampires but does not kill the yielding methuselah. (outcome : contesting is bad, but not deadly)
> contesting can be a strategy (If A plays Stanislava, that she is downed to a few bloods, then B contests Stanislava. A will ponder "do I yield now or lose transfers to gain some pool?")

A few cases to illustrate what this suggestion can lead to :
-A plays stanislava, B stops influencing her, then plays another
vampire. B is slowed, A plays with stanislava, her blood drops down,
then B contests : the benefit of having played with a contested
vampire will be balanced by the fact the vampire has less blood.
-A and B play stanislava. A uses the new influence rule, but just has
Nadima and another stanislava to influence on to. If he keeps
buggering B he will contest stanislava again. If he's smart and if he
wants to play, he will play Nadima and loose 3 blood in the process,
plus the 1 pool burned to keep contesting. So, as I said, contesting
is still bad with this rule.

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
I am very interested in LSJ's thinking about the transfer back rule.

I agree with him that that transferring back and 'unique-crypt-lottery-
loss' are connected discussions, because you cannot talk about getting
rid of 'transferring back' without also talking about changing the
rule for cypt contestation. Transferring back is the most basic
mitigation for 'unique-crypt-lottery-loss' that the game provides.

From my experience crypt contestation or its threat happens at a more
than negligible rate. I estimate I've played 50 games since getting
back into the game in October 08, and I can think of six games in
which vampires were contested or could have been contested.

Nonetheless, I don't have a strong objection to the current vampire
contestation rule. My only criticism is that it could be more
dynamic. Losing the use of a vampire to contestation or losing pool
and transfers to 'unique-crypt-lottery-loss' can greatly reduce a
player's options, especially in the case of big vampires. This makes
the game less fun. I am more interested in the transferring back
rules, but if I had to change the vampire contestation rules to the
game more fun, the options I would prefer would be:
1. Open uncontrolled regions and keeping traditional contestation.
This gives players' full knowledge of the possibility of
contestation. All players can begin adapting to the table environment
starting with turn one.
2. Dynamic vampire contestation. Whenever a player influences a
unique vampire (or imbued, etc.) from the uncontrolled region, if
another copy of that vampire is in play, it is returned to its owner's
uncontrolled region like a Banishment. This could still hose the
contesting players, but it would allow for more interesting strategic
play. It fits the flavor of the VTES gameworld well: two (or more?)
Methusalehs invest resources to influence the same key vampire, whose
allegiance changes according to which Methusaleh most recently exerted
the necessary influence.

Removing transferring back: in recent posts on Extrala.blogspot.com
( http://extrala.blogspot.com/2009/07/results-poll-would-you-like-to-see.html
), I have argued in favor of removing the transferring back rule. I
think getting rid of 'transferring back' would be interesting because:
1. Transferring back has become a bloat tool, although it was
originally intended to mitigate potential contestations. The
roleplaying concept expressed by superior Govern the Unaligned and
Enchant Kindred is not one of gaining general resources; the concept
is using your controlled vampires' mind control powers to bring more
vampires under your control. I think it's better for game mechanics
to conform to the flavor of the cards.
2. Removing transferring back would balance the power of Presence and
especially Dominate to other disciplines. Yes, that means weakening
them.
3. Removing transferring back would speed up games because there would
be fewer bloat options.
4. It doesn't make sense to be able to transfer resources rather
easily away from a vampire you don't control, while it requires a card
(Blood Doll, Minion Tap, etc.) to get resources away from a vampire
you do control. I used the example of bribing an official in my post
on extrala.blogspot. I guess LSJ is talking about this issue in other
posts as well. http://extrala.blogspot.com/2009/08/poll-transfer-rules-change-proposal.html

BTW: Why is this topic called "Ban Rush" now?

be made". It's true that if you play a mono-deck (like, turbo cybele
CotGB, or the polemic turbo Ian Forestal :p) and you are contested,
it's still a serious issue. However, if you do not have a plan B, it's
because you chose that weakness. Since you, as both player and
deckbuilder haven't thought about a backplan, you've got to pay the
price of that decision. And anyway, any deck will have a blindspot.
This solution takes just a line or two in the rulebook, and does not
affect general gameplay since vampire contesting is a cornercase.

One more thing : library cards contesting is a more frequent issue and
the harsh old way of dealing with it works fine, if you ask me, and I
doubt many players find it unbalanced. I think it's better to have a
general rule for contests and then an additional option to give a
lifesaver to contesters.

mate ;) ), the main concern I have is about "coming into controlled
region effects" (like Tariq, Anarch Convert, and so on and so forth.)
The fact is, a lot of rulings already exist, and just need to be
checked out and updated, and I don't think many of them will need
changes. I hope LSJ will find my proposition and will like it, if he
still reads this troll of a topic.

The rush deck is expending resources to tac-nuke a minion. There is a
clear loss for the controller for the minion. There is a clear cost to
the rush deck. There is a clear gain for everybody else at the table
just because they happened to sit there.

Don't forget that because of the seating, you are guaranteed to be in
an unintentional situation (e.g. if you went light with your combat
package to have more punch with your actions, the last thing you want
is to sit at the same table with a rush deck; you could say that being
there to begin with is quite unintentional).

If players play cleverly, contestation becomes a tactical tool. I've
seen more games being upset by trigger-happy combat decks rushing
willy-nilly, wreaking havoc and then dying, then contestation. By a
magnitude of something like a lot. Really.

If anything, we should change the seating - let each player decide
where to sit, with perfect information about each opponent's deck,
to make sure nobody has to have the frustrating experience of going
too heavy / too light on some aspect of the game (or repeating some
key crypt card). :)

strongest discplines, and have the most ways to bloat via transferring
back. Removing the transfer-back rule would weaken cards like Govern
the Unaligned and Enchant Kindred, which is a good thing for game
balance.

That said, I think there are other ways to make Dominate more
balanced, and removing the transfer back rule isn't the way I'd go
about it.

I agree with other posters who have noted that in regular gameplay, I
often use the transfer back rule to put some pool on a fatty; if I
oust my prey, I'll add more and bring out the minion. If things go
badly, I'll transfer back. It has nothing to do with contesting or
bloating. I will often use the transfer back rule to bloat, and
practically never related to contesting (since contesting rarely
happens.)

Ira

> player to remove that card from the game and redistribute the blood counters on

>
> Coupled with a similar rule for contested cards: When yielding a crypt card,
> redistribute <as above>.

As noted earlier in the thread, this is likely to make cards such as
Banishment and Reality somewhat stronger. I propose the following
addition to help mitigate this power:

A methuselah may forfeit his transfers for the turn in order to get
two gransfers instead. Each gransfer may be spent to move one blood
from an uncontrolled minion to that methuselah's pool.

This rule would also have some side effects. For example, a methuselah
who has invested pool in a minion on one turn, but decides on a later
turn that another minion would be a better choice, to eventually
reclaim the initial investment. I think that this is a beneficial
effect in general because, unlike library cards - where the cost is
paid all at once, and the card takes effect immediately - crypt cards
are often purchased in installments, and remain completely unusable
until the entire cost is paid. This can leave a methuselah in the
awkward position of having a great deal of his resources invested in a
card that he becomes unable to use. Certainly, one could take the
position that a player who moved 4 pool onto an 8-capacity vampire and
ended up with less than 5 pool on his next turn, unable to afford the
remaining influence, deserves his fate. However, I would instead argue
that whatever reduced this player from a percieved-comfortable pool
total to less than 5 pool was probably a sufficiently bad fate without
requiring that the player's 4 pool investment remain locked in limbo
forever.

It would also have the side effect of allowing cards such as
Ecoterrorists and Art Museum to be used for poolgain instead of just
bringing out additional minions. I think this effect is probably
acceptable, given the current state of the game. It would allow
certain kinds of decks to go lighter on defense than normal, relying
on a steady drip of poolgain to counteract a portion of their
predator's offense, but I don't think it badly throws off the game
balance compared to the benefits. Maybe Govern the Unaligned would be
a little too good, but that's a hit I'd be willing to take.

-witness1

Messages.Author: Ira Fay
Messages.Body:
On Aug 18, 6:41 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
> If extra bloat is not good for the game:
> Replace the undo influence rule (i.e., two transfers to move a counter from
> uncontrolled to pool) with:
>
> Expose a crypt card that would contest a unique card controlled by another
> player to remove that card from the game and redistribute the blood counters on
> that card among your other uncontrolled minions and/or your pool.
>
> Coupled with a similar rule for contested cards: When yielding a crypt card,
> redistribute <as above>.

The proposed rule above would significantly lessen the consequences of
being in the unlucky position of contesting a crypt card with another
player. Nice improvement!

Unfortunately, the rule above also has a large impact on two other
strategies (which both occur much more often than contesting crypt
cards):
1) Partially transferring onto a crypt card with the possibility of
bringing it out the following turn. For example, I might put 2 onto a
6-cap, then decide whether or not to bring out the minion next turn.
Using the undo influence rule I can reclaim the 2 pool, or spend 4
more to bring it out.

2) Gaining pool through cards that add counters directly to cards in
the uncontrolled region. This is a significant defensive element of
the game, and it's rare to play a game where this doesn't occur.

Perhaps you would consider keeping the undo influence rule, and simply
adding the 2 contesting-related rules you mention above? That way,
you still address the rare case of contesting, but you don't eliminate
the interesting strategies of #1 and #2 that I list above.

It seems to me that cards like Grooming the Protege or Flames of
Insurrection are well-balanced given the defensive options in #2. If
we remove the defensive option in #2, then many cards become weaker,
which means they will get played less, which makes the game overall
less interesting IMO. One of the things that I love about VTES is the
diversity of viable decks, and I'm reluctant to support any change
that would reduce the number of playable cards.

IMO, bloat in the form of the undo influence rule isn't broken,
because it usually max's out at 2 pool per turn. It's an interesting
element of defense, but a good predator will do more than 2 pool
damage per turn. If the actual design problem that you're trying to
fix is, "the game is too slow" (i.e. "extra bloat is not good for the
game"), then why not try a more direct change, like "gain 10 pool and
a VP for an oust" ? Removing one of many defensive options won't
address the fundamental issue that players have a strong incentive not
to get ousted.

Thanks for listening,
Ira

Messages.Author: Mark
Messages.Body:


Out of sheer interest: this whole discussion started because the
punishment (consequences) of contesting can be quite harsh, and might
need some form of change in the rules so that the (unintended)
punishment doesn't have such a huge impact on one's game of V:tes,
agreed?

It appears to be difficult to come up with such a change, without
changing something else as well (so far, bloat / poolmanagement always
seems to pop up as being a source of unwanted effects - not so strange
since poolmanagement is exaclty what we're fooling around with here).

So far, concerning contesting, the following situations may occur:

1) Contesting a unique library card: this invites for tactical play
(in game-terms: two methuselahs wish to make use of unique *whatever*
and neither of them gets to until the other forfeits).

2) Purpously (tactically) contesting a crypt card: the kind of
contesting where you get to decide to start influencing a crypt card
of which you know someone else already controls (because it's in play
already, for example) - a mechanic that occurs when you wish to take
away your prey's last blocker or whatever other reason you might have
for the intended contest.

3) Accidentally contesting a crypt card (the UFO-melting-rock-paper-
scissor-with-laser-beam occurrance - I had such a laugh about this
comparison...): the contesting of a crypt card two folks started to
influence without knowing the other's intent.

Ad. 1 - I think we all agree this doesn't need a rule change, since
most of the time it doesn't involve a lot of pool or a card that much
needed in a deck that it cannot continue without it.

Ad. 2 - I'm not sure if this form of contesting needs a rule-change. I
stated that, in this case, someone starts influencing a minion that is
already in play. So if it's a low-cap minion, it will not have such a
big impact on your game, since you have probably more of them out. In
case of the contest taking away your last blocker; you've been
tactically ousted - wooo to your predator for smart play. If it's a
high-cap minion, it's gonna take multiple turns to get on the table,
and you will have some time working on more defense. So impact may be
bigger, but you should still be able to play since your support cast
may be out as well (didn't bring support cast; you made a bad decision
and it's your own fault things went bad - I know I am a bit blunt
here...). Situation I don't think needs a rule-change.

Ad. 3 - Not knowing someone else is influencing the same minion can
really fuck up the game, for either of the methuselahs involved in the
contesting, especially if it's the first you try to bring out. Even in
the previously described situation where you bring out a high-cap
minion, and then someone else brings out the same minion in his next
turn and states "sorry mate, we're contesting, but I need this guy for
my deck". Even though it might be a bit of an asshat statement; the
guy still didn't know you were going to bring out the same minion as
he. So either way, you both (or at least one of you) gets screwed
because of sheer coincidence / bad lottery draw / whatever you will
call it. This situation is the one that might need a change in ruling.

I hope I made clear the difference in situation in each of the above
examples.

Now my question is - is it even possible to separate these situations
so that only the last one will benefit from a change in rules?

The suggestion of revealing a contested minion and redistribute the
pool to other cryptcards or your pool still seems viable to me, and I
fail to see how a card like GtU can be greatly abused in a situation
like this.

The situation that needs attention is already a very rare occasion
(think everyone agrees on that too), so how the proposed solution to
this problem could be intentionally abused is beyond me.

Worst case scenario: someone has a 5 cap in play. I have the same one
in my crypt. I use GtU in a correct way and move three counters to the
card. Later I influence two more, I reveal the card, state it's
contesting, and redistribute the counters to a 10 cap which wasn't a
viable target for the GtU in the first place. I assume this is the
kind of abuse as described a couple of times in this thread.

Now in this case, since everyone on the table can see to what card I
am influencing, everyone would really know the difference between a
coincidal contest, or my atempt to abuse a change in the rules, right?

So the question still stands: is it possible to separate these
situations so that only the last one will benefit from a change in
rules? Because if it is, it seems to me that the proposed change (by I
think it was LSJ who made it up) the problem will be solved.

What am I missing here?

Depending on your bloat preference, the proposal is

EITHER

Extend influence both to controlled and to contested vampires.

OR

Replace the undo influence rule (i.e., two transfers to move a counter from
uncontrolled to pool) with:

Expose a crypt card that would contest a unique card controlled by another
player to remove that card from the game and redistribute the blood counters on
that card among your other uncontrolled minions and/or your pool.

Coupled with a similar rule for contested cards: When yielding a crypt card,
redistribute <as above>.

(and some verbiage to handle external Banishment-like effects similarly)

>> 1) Partially transferring onto a crypt card with the possibility of
>> bringing it out the following turn. For example, I might put 2 onto a
>> 6-cap, then decide whether or not to bring out the minion next turn.
>> Using the undo influence rule I can reclaim the 2 pool, or spend 4
>> more to bring it out.
>

It seems unfortunate to me that we lose something that was described in
the Jyhad rulebook as a real possibility. In the Jyhad rulebook, Nora
changes her mind over her investment.

Apparently, the designers had considered this possibility and thought it
was a good idea. Presumably, they had realized and considered that the
transfer-back option could be used for this, not just defeating the
problems that contesting unique vampires brought to bear.

Clearly, Nora's actions still have consequences - she is 2 pool down for
the duration of the time it is on the "wrong" vampire - but the
consequences aren't irrevocable.

Perhaps one of the lessons they learned from the contested vampire
situation was that irrevocable decisions regarding vampires weren't a
good idea more generally. In the very early game, you can make bad
decisions because there is no information (in many situations,
certainly). It's that lack of information that can cause the
contestation issues they were resolving - I have 8 pool on Lazarus, you
bring out yours before me, neither of us knew what the other was doing.
The transfer back rules can also potentially compensate for the lack of
information in other situations - I start bringing out a big vampire,
find that my predator is about to swarm me, change my mind and bring out
some of my weenies, and bring that pool back from Saulot when I get the
chance. Or the other way round - Nora might well be bringing pool back
from an part-influenced weenie to bring Saulot out, once her grand-
predator has crippled her predator.

This mind-changing possibility seems to have been intended in the final
rules, even if an earlier draft of the rules lacked it.

Removing a strategic option that the original designers introduced into
the game seems unfortunate, unless it's breaking the game somehow. The
ability to change your mind on influencing doesn't seem to be breaking
the game currently.

--
James Coupe

Sure. That's fine if they were in a closed system in fixed supply.

But that's not the case here. Resources are put into play freely from an
unlimited supply (the bank).

Pool tends to be more important and therefore harder to generate spontaneously,
in contrast to blood which is less important and can be generated easily.

Counters on uncontrolled minions are generated fairly easily, like blood on the
minion rather than pool in your pool.

But the undo influence rule breaks down that distinction (unnecessarily, given
what it was introduced to do), letting the easily available blood leak more
freely into the pool.

> To be sure, 1:1 instantaneous conversion destroys strategy. 1:0 does
> as well. If only there could be some middle ground, where resources
> can be converted and shuffled, but at some cost to the player.

Yes. And the cost for this pool doesn't seem to be in line with the rest.

As I mentioned in my original post, I believe such a change would be
unfortunate. The reason it's unfortunate is because it would reduce
the strategic depth* of the game.

* "Strategic depth" is related to both the number of choices available
to a player at any time and the consequences of those choices.

LSJ seems to be focusing on the consequences of those choices, but I
believe number of choices available matters too. If we remove the
option to transfer back from a partially-influenced minion, we remove
choice from the player (and increase the consequences of making a poor
influence decision.) Personally, I think the consequences of making a
poor partial-influence decision are already harsh enough, and I see no
need to make them harsher, but that's just my opinion of the way the
game currently plays.

> > 2) Gaining pool through cards that add counters directly to cards in
> > the uncontrolled region.  This is a significant defensive element of
> > the game, and it's rare to play a game where this doesn't occur.
>
> Again not unfortunate.
>
> See also the "loss" of the ability to use transfers to pull counters from
> controlled vampires simply because the undo influence rule had the restriction
> "uncontrolled" on it.

I believe losing such a defensive strategy would be bad for the game,
because it will make many cards less playable, and decrease deck
variety.

As a general design philosophy of a CCG, I believe that changing
fundamental rules of the game should only be undertaken if a
significant improvement would be made. As far as I can tell, no one
in this thread (other than LSJ who may be playing devil's advocate)
seems to think that the game would benefit from removing the undo
influence rule.

What is the benefit that would be achieved? I see the following
impacts, among others:
- Greater consequences for poor partial-influence decisions = Bad for
the game IMO
- Reduced choices available to the player in the influence phase = Bad
for the game IMO
- Removal of a defensive option (pool gain through transferring back)
= Bad for the game IMO
- Easier decisions during the influence phase -> faster decisions ->
faster games = Good for the game IMO
- Old rulebooks are no longer correct, must teach old players
returning to the game another rules change = Bad for the game IMO
- Govern the Unaligned is weaker = Good for the game IMO
- Flames of Insurrection is weaker = Bad for the game IMO

And the list goes on. I'm curious to hear what LSJ sees as some of
the largest benefits (and largest drawbacks) of removing the undo
influence rule. And if he's just playing devil's advocate and isn't
seriously considering making this change, then I'd rather just let
this issue drop and stop worrying about it. But at the moment, I feel
like LSJ is seriously considering removing the undo influence rule,
and I currently think that change would be bad for the game.

> > Perhaps you would consider keeping the undo influence rule, and simply
> > adding the 2 contesting-related rules you mention above?
>
> Considered, of course.
>
> With the result that, since they are both introduced to address the same
> contesting issues, both are not needed.

I disagree. Regardless of why the rules were introduced, the current
state of VTES is that the undo influence rule doesn't address the high
consequences of contesting crypt cards, but it does allow for
interesting choices during deck building and the influence phase.

Therefore, it's possible to add the 2 contesting-related rules LSJ
mentioned without changing the undo influence rule. By adding the
contesting rules, we fix the problem with contesting crypt cards, and
by leaving the undo influence rule, we leave the strategic depth that
it provides.

> > That way,
> > you still address the rare case of contesting, but you don't eliminate
> > the interesting strategies of #1 and #2 that I list above.
>
> Then what about the interesting strategies that are lost by restricting undo
> influence to uncontrolled?

I would be happy to consider the strategic depth that would be added
by allowing influence to controlled minions. Off the top of my head:
Blood Doll and Vessel would be a lot less useful. It would be a lot
less risky to spend pool to bring out more minions. Cards that give
you more transfers would become much more valuable. The influence
phase would take a lot longer, since there would be so many more
choices. It would be a significant change to explain to old players
returning to the game.

I'd rather expand influence to controlled minions than remove the undo
influence rule. But I'd most prefer to make neither change, since
making any large rule change has a large default negative value IMO;
it obsoletes old rulebooks and makes the game harder to learn for
returning players.

> Of course, any card that uses the rule being changed or removed will be affected.
>
> It doesn't necessarily make the game less interesting, of course, as other uses
> may be examined and/or players will use more strategy regarding resource management.

I agree that making a rules change doesn't necessarily make the game
less interesting. In this particular case, when I consider removing
the undo influence rule, I believe it would actually make the game
less interesting, for the reasons I stated above.

Thanks for listening,
Ira

P.S. I'd like to take a moment to acknowledge how incredible it is
that the lead game designer of this game is having an ongoing design
conversation with the player base. It's really amazing, and I deeply
appreciate it. Thank you, LSJ!

Messages.Author: witness1
Messages.Body:
On Aug 20, 3:45 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
> witness1 wrote:
> > Funny. I tend to think of the ability to shuffle and convert resources
> > as PART of resource management.
>
> Sure. That's fine if they were in a closed system in fixed supply.
>
> But that's not the case here. Resources are put into play freely from an
> unlimited supply (the bank).

Some kinds are unlimited, sure. Blood from hunting. Others require
card text to achieve this end, and are otherwise restricted to the 30
starting pool, up to 90 library cards, and 12 or more crypt cards.
Plus the Edge.

I'm not sure any of that meets the criteria for "freely".

> Pool tends to be more important and therefore harder to generate spontaneously,
> in contrast to blood which is less important and can be generated easily.
>
> Counters on uncontrolled minions are generated fairly easily, like blood on the
> minion rather than pool in your pool.

In some cases, the opposite is true (Grooming the Protege vs. Minion
Tap).

I'll grant that it is usually easier to generate counters on
uncontrolled minions than pool, but dispute that it is like blood on
the minion. Art Museum puts counters only on Toreador; Society Hunting
Ground puts counters on any ready vampire. Enchant Kindred requires a
superior discipline to put 2 counters on an uncontrolled minion;
Restoration puts the same amount on a ready vampire at inferior, gains
one extra at superior. Hunting is a +1 stealth rulebook action, no
methuselah can put counters from the bank on uncontrolled minions
without card text.

> But the undo influence rule breaks down that distinction (unnecessarily, given
> what it was introduced to do), letting the easily available blood leak more
> freely into the pool.

Possibly.

> > To be sure, 1:1 instantaneous conversion destroys strategy. 1:0 does
> > as well. If only there could be some middle ground, where resources
> > can be converted and shuffled, but at some cost to the player.
>
> Yes. And the cost for this pool doesn't seem to be in line with the rest.

I'm not sure that's generally true. Consider playing a hunting ground
+ a Blood Doll to generate one pool per turn with minimal impact on
the rest of your game - no cost to your actions or your transfers.
Similarly, consider playing Arcane Library + Information Highway to
achieve the same effect with the same relatve impact - 2 pool, 2 MPAs,
no net change of transfers, no net change in actions per turn.

This is a simplistic analysis, to be sure - each combination has
strengths and weaknesses beyond the specific goal of gaining pool.
Specifically, transfers tend to be plentiful in supply once your pool
total has reduced to a point where buying investing in your current
crop of uncontrolled minions becomes foolhardy. Something else to do
with transfers - such as removing one of your contestable minions in
an attempt to replace it with an affordable one - could help mitigate
that fact.

Regardless of all that, if the cost actually is out of line with the
effect, it should be fixed without regard to changes in contestation.
If false, it should remain unchanged regardless of contestation
changes. After all, the rule doesn't appear to be serving it's purpose
of mitigating the consequences of contestation (and even if it is, we
seem plenty capable of coming up with alternatives).

-witness1

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
Please add my vote in favor of removing "transfer back".

My main objection to transferring back is that it is unfaithful to
world being described within the card game. It hurts the flavor of
the game.

An ancient vampire (the Methusaleh) who uses resources in a bid to
influence or control a younger vampire would not be able to recuperate
that investment without first totally controlling the vampire. Like
investing money to start a business or time to complete a project, you
can't recuperate your investment until the enterprise is completed.

Using Dominate and Presence cards to gain pool is not faithful to what
those cards represent. The cards represent a vampire using their
mental powers to sway a younger vampire to their Methusaleh's cause.
Right now the Methusaleh can somehow gain general resources by
relinquishing this partial mental control.

I certainly use the transfer back rule for bloating when I can, but it
weakens the flavor of the game. It makes the influence phase
mechanical, with less room to describe a game-world concept. Making
the CCG mechanics reflect game world concepts as well as possible
makes the game stronger and more interesting to me.

Another positive is that removing transferring back would probably
speed up game times.

Removing the transfer back rules still leaves room for new cards that
allow you to transfer back from uncontrolled vampires, but as a card
function, not a basic game function:

Relinquish the Reins
Master
Remove all blood from cards in your uncontrolled region into the blood
pool. Add a number equal to half the blood removed (rounding down)
into your pool.

Messages.Author: Ira Fay
Messages.Body:
On Aug 21, 12:33 am, Mark <markangel1...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On 20 aug, 22:22, Ira Fay <ira...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > As I mentioned in my original post, I believe such a change would be
> > unfortunate.  The reason it's unfortunate is because it would reduce
> > the strategic depth* of the game.
>
> I don't agree. Don't even see what you're talking about. How would it
> 'reduce strategic depth'?

I'll try again.

Strategic Depth is defined by number of choices available and the
consequences of those choices. There are also other factors, but
those are the two big contributors to strategic depth.

If you remove the undo influence rule, there are fewer choices for the
player during the influence phase, and therefore strategic depth is
reduced.

It seems like you're saying: This change would weaken Govern the
Unaligned [I agree], and therefore a greater diversity of cards,
disciplines, and deck types will be played [I disagree.]

Even though Govern the Unaligned will be weaker under the proposed
rule, it will still be plenty strong to play it for the bleed and
influence acceleration. Many other cards that are interesting
(Grooming the Protege, Flames of Insurrection) will also be weakened,
but likely weakened to the point of not seeing play.

Decks will still need to defend themselves under the proposed rule;
it's simply that bloat via +1 or +2 pool during the influence phase
will no longer be possible. Decks that were previously relying on
that type of defense will no longer be viable. Since this rule
doesn't add any new or interesting defensive options, I believe that
fewer new deck types will be created. We'll simply see more focused
decks.

I infer from LSJ's posts that he thinks the game is too slow, or
rewards sitting back and waiting too much. I think that point has a
lot of weight. But, I don't think the solution is removing
interesting defensive strategies. Personally, I think Govern and
Powerbase: Montreal are interesting, because they require actions or
provide table actions, all of which create interaction. If I were the
designer, I'd experiment with stronger incentives for ousting, like
+10 pool instead of +6 pool. Or maybe 6+X, where X is the number of
players remaining the game after the oust.

And if there is a problem with bloat via uncontrolled (and I don't
think there is), then create a card like:

The Winnowing
Burn an uncontrolled minion in your prey's uncontrolled region as a
(D) action that costs X blood, where X is the amount of blood on that
card; any blood on that card is returned to your prey's pool.

Ira

"Ira Fay" <ira...@gmail.com> wrote in message news:43aa3167-96f8-4a4f...@l5g2000pra.googlegroups.com...

> I infer from LSJ's posts that he thinks the game is too slow, or

I don't know if he thinks that. But I've thought that for quite a
long time.

> I think that point has a
> lot of weight. But, I don't think the solution is removing
> interesting defensive strategies. Personally, I think Govern and
> Powerbase: Montreal are interesting, because they require actions or
> provide table actions, all of which create interaction.

Agree with you about Powerbase: Montreal. I'm not so sure about Govern
the Unaligned because the guy who uses it to bloat typically will
construct his deck to make sure that it's usually effective and hence,
although he might pay the price in other ways, I don't see how this
"creates interaction" in any strong way.

> If I were the
> designer, I'd experiment with stronger incentives for ousting, like
> +10 pool instead of +6 pool. Or maybe 6+X, where X is the number of
> players remaining the game after the oust.

I don't think that would be a worthwhile direction in which to tinker.
The rewards for ousting are fine; the problem is that 1) VtES is the
kind of multiplayer game which is suseptible to the "gang-up" factor
that tends to balance and hence stablize play in response to a player
who makes good progress against his goals; and 2) the available cards
and rules facilitate this sort of balancing too much. As a result,
good players will typically think defense and staying in the game
first and offense, ousting, and nailing down victory points only when
and where there survival is pretty much assured. There are certainly
exceptions to this, but on the whole I've always found play tilted too
much towards defense.

Adding some pool as reward for oust doesn't effect this equation much
as far as I can see. You still can't collect it if you're dead and to
the extent it rewards a successful oust, it will also have a lot of
balancing tendency to make players defensive based on the reasoning
that their predator would _likewise_ be rewarded for ousting them
and so they better be on their toes to prevent it. Cancel cancel.
What it would really do is tend to destablize play more after each
oust and this doesn't strike me as a positive thing. IMHO play after
each oust is destablized about right: the ousting player is rewarded
with good momentum but it isn't a slam dunk for them to go on and
sweep - and that's exactly as it should be.

The problem, IMHO, is that play can get too stable _before_ ousts are
made. To counter this tendency, I'm not too sure exactly what the
game needs but it's probably good to look at the kinds of things that
currently tend to destablize play outside of an oust. For instance,
Week of Nightmares and Palla Grande with weenies tends to do it.
In general, any kind of weeny build-up strategy seems to force play,
although a lot of those things have been forestalled due to the
unpopularity of weeny decks in the game. I understand why that's so,
but it gives us a clue about what kinds of cards might be worth
designing to encourage less stability in play: cards that have some
element of extreme but temporary advantages (or disadvantages when
played on a prey might also work).

> And if there is a problem with bloat via uncontrolled (and I don't
> think there is),

There's a million ways to build the deck that just bloats successfully -
at the cost of any ability to do anything else. Generally, the cost
tends to be too high to make these decks worth building. To the
extent that such decks are worth building, the answer would be to
saddle the key card(s) involved with more disadvantage (or ban them
entirely).

Fred

The ability to partially influence vampires of capacity greater than 4
mid-game without the spent pool becoming completely unretrievable will
not be replaced by any new strategic option. Certainly, the game
